newsitem.title: UK: RUGBY UNION-FIVE NATIONS RIVALS SEEK LIFT-OFF.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-FIVE NATIONS RIVALS SEEK LIFT-OFF.

text.p: England and Wales have a rare opportunity to spread their wings and escape the shackles of Five Nations' championship history this weekend at Scotland and Ireland's expense.

For the first time in five years, the tournament opened with two away wins and the two victims, the Scots and the Irish, are still hunting for form and confidence as they reassemble for potentially barren visits to Twickenham and Cardiff Arms Park respectively.

England, champions for the last two seasons, and Wales, suddenly breathing fire again with the return of their rugby league exiles, are strong favourites to make home advantage count and a Triple Crown decider is already looming in Cardiff in March.

Such a black-and-white scenario, however, is not a Five Nations speciality and there are numerous precedents which suggest a colourful upset or two may not be beyond the realms of possibility on Saturday.

England, for example, are chasing a record eighth successive win over the Scots but have not managed to score a try against their oldest opponents since 1993, a sad reflection on the brand of rugby the fixture has generated in recent years.

They also needed a last-gasp score to squeeze past Argentina in their last outing and coach Jack Rowell is telling anyone prepared to listen that his side are in the middle of a major rebuilding operation.
Scotland, by their captain Rob Wainwright's admission, let their country down with their second-half performance against Wales, but Rowell is expecting a more determined side to appear at Twickenham.
"The Scots will be on the rebound," he said. "They have to win to be in with a chance of winning the championship so doubtless we'll see what I call the 'blue shirt effect.'
"When they pull on a blue shirt, they become bigger men and a resilient team, not least when they play England."
To remind the younger players of their historical responsibilities, Rowell called on former captain Will Carling to brief his team mates on how to handle Saturday's test.

"We asked Will to put the Five Nations into focus, particularly playing against the Scots," revealed Rowell. "He stressed the point that the Five Nations is different to any of the games we played before Christmas."
Scotland will have learnt from watching Brive hustle Martin Johnson out of the line-outs in the European Cup final last weekend, leading directly to Leicester's downfall.
Something similar happened against the Pumas and England, seeking a more reliable escape route should things go wrong again, have ditched Mike Catt at fly-half and gone for Paul Grayson instead.
"They seem to have picked a side to win rather than to entertain," said Wainwright. "But this time Dean Richards is missing which we're happy about. Whenever he's been involved, we've lost."
Astonishingly, the last Welsh home win over Ireland was 14 years ago, conclusive proof that Five Nations results remain a law unto themselves.

Both sides have had injury problems in the lead-up to their latest encounter, with pressure on New Zealand-born debutant hooker Ross Nesdale to fill the big gap left by injured Irish captain Keith Wood.
Wales have also lost their influential centre Allan Bateman and have spent most of the build-up to Saturday monitoring the state of Robert Howley's injured shoulder.

Wood, Howley and Bateman, along with Scott Quinnell and Scott Gibbs, have probably already done enough to secure places on the Lions tour of South Africa, but the battle of the respective packs should unearth a few more candidates.
Players on all sides will be interested to see how southern hemisphere referees Paddy O'Brien and Wayne Erickson react on their Five Nations debuts.
New Zealander O'Brien, in particular, has the tough task of coaxing some flowing rugby out of the England-Scotland grudge match, with neutrals everywhere praying he succeeds.
